page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claim_text: Most breast symptoms are not cancer, but they should still be assessed properly.

primary_source.title: Breast cancer - symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, risk

evidence_summary: healthdirect states 'most breast lumps are not cancerous' while advising review. The article pairs the reassurance with a clear instruction to have symptoms assessed, which matches authoritative advice.
limitations: Reassurance is appropriate but is deliberately balanced with 'should still be assessed properly', avoiding a false-reassurance risk. No harm identified.
reviewer_notes: Well-balanced reassurance-plus-action wording. Low AHPRA risk. Retain the 'but should still be assessed' clause on any future edit so it never reads as bare reassurance.

page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claim_text: screening mammograms are for people without symptoms. A new lump or change needs diagnostic assessment, not just routine screening.
evidence_summary: BreastScreen is an asymptomatic screening program; symptomatic patients require diagnostic assessment (triple test) rather than screening. This distinction is central to safe care-seeking and is correctly stated.
limitations: Care-affecting claim: correctly steers symptomatic patients away from screening-only pathways toward diagnostic assessment. This reduces, rather than creates, harm.
reviewer_notes: Strong, defensible wording. This is the safest framing and should be preserved.

page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claim_text: Triple assessment: A breast assessment approach that may include examination, imaging and biopsy when needed.
evidence_summary: Triple assessment (clinical examination, imaging, and biopsy/pathology when indicated) is the standard breast symptom work-up in Australian practice. The 'may include ... when needed' hedge is accurate.
limitations: Definition-level statement; appropriately hedged.

page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claim_text: The BreastScreen Australia Program targets women aged 50 to 74, while some others may be eligible.

supporting_source.org: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
supporting_source.title: Who should have a breast screen

evidence_summary: Verified current: BreastScreen Australia actively invites women aged 50-74 for free 2-yearly mammograms; women aged 40-49 and 75+ are eligible for free screening but are not sent invitations. The article's 'targets 50 to 74, while some others may be eligible' is accurate and does not overstate.
limitations: Program ages can change; verify at each review. The article correctly signals 'ask your GP what applies to you', avoiding an absolute eligibility claim.
reviewer_notes: Dept of Health page (supporting_source) returned HTTP 503 on direct fetch on the verification date; content confirmed via Cancer Council Australia (which mirrors the program) and via search snapshot of the Dept page. Re-verify the Dept URL resolves at next review. This is a change-prone program rule - keep the 12-month review cadence.

page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claim_text: BreastScreen is for screening people without symptoms. A new lump or change should be assessed by a GP so diagnostic imaging can be arranged if needed.
evidence_summary: Consistent with WHS-02; reinforces that symptomatic presentations need diagnostic assessment, not screening. Accurate.
limitations: None material.

page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claim_text: Breast pain is common and often not cancer, but persistent, one-sided or worrying pain should be assessed.

primary_source.title: Breast cancer - symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, risk

evidence_summary: Mastalgia is a common, usually benign presentation; breast pain alone is an uncommon presenting feature of breast cancer. The claim is accurate and appropriately paired with a 'should be assessed' safety net.
limitations: Uses 'common' without quantification, but the statement is epidemiologically accurate and balanced with an assessment prompt, so no false reassurance.

page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claim_text: Should I check my own breasts? It is helpful to know what is normal for you and seek review if you notice a new or persistent change.
evidence_summary: Current Australian guidance favours 'breast awareness' (knowing what is normal for you and reporting changes) over formal routine breast self-examination technique. The article uses the breast-awareness framing correctly and avoids over-promising a self-exam benefit.
limitations: None material; framing aligns with the shift away from prescriptive self-examination.
reviewer_notes: Good - avoids overstating benefit of self-examination.

page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claim_text: In Australia, routine screening looks for HPV, the virus that causes most cervical cancers.
evidence_summary: The renewed National Cervical Screening Program uses a primary HPV test; HPV is described by Cancer Council as 'the main cause of cervical cancer' (persistent oncogenic HPV underlies almost all cases). 'Causes most cervical cancers' is accurate and conservatively worded.
limitations: 'Most' is a conservative phrasing (HPV is implicated in ~99% of cases); no overstatement.

page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claim_text: The National Cervical Screening Program invites women and people with a cervix aged 25 to 74 to have a Cervical Screening Test every five years through a healthcare provider.

supporting_source.org: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
supporting_source.title: About the National Cervical Screening Program

evidence_summary: Verified current: eligible people aged 25-74 with a cervix are invited to a 5-yearly HPV-based Cervical Screening Test. Ages and interval match the program exactly.
limitations: Change-prone program rule; verify ages/interval each review. Dept of Health page returned HTTP 503 on direct fetch; confirmed via Cancer Council Australia and search snapshot.
reviewer_notes: Re-verify the Dept URL resolves at next review. Keep 12-month cadence for this program rule.

page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claim_text: Many eligible patients can now choose self-collection ... Eligible patients can collect their own vaginal sample in a private space after instructions from a healthcare provider.

supporting_source.org: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
supporting_source.title: Self-collection for cervical screening

evidence_summary: Since 1 July 2022 self-collection of a vaginal sample has been available to all screen-eligible people aged 25-74 who choose it, accessed through a healthcare provider; it is as effective at detecting HPV as a clinician-collected sample. Article wording ('many eligible patients', 'after instructions from a healthcare provider') is accurate.
limitations: The article correctly notes eligibility and that self-collection is arranged via a provider; it does not overstate universal availability without provider involvement.
reviewer_notes: Consider (optional) adding that self-collection is now offered to all screening participants who choose it, not only a subset - current 'many eligible patients' slightly understates availability but is not incorrect. No change required. Dept of Health self-collection page returned 503 on direct fetch; corroborated by Cancer Council and search snapshot.

page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claim_text: Do I need screening if I have had the HPV vaccine? Yes. HPV vaccination reduces risk but does not replace cervical screening.
evidence_summary: Cancer Council states 'whether you've had the HPV vaccine or not, regular screening remains essential'. The claim is accurate and important for safe care-seeking.
limitations: None material.
reviewer_notes: No change needed - this is a key safety message.

page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claim_text: Cervical screening is one of the most important preventive health checks for women and people with a cervix.
recommended_wording: Cervical screening is one of the most effective ways to help prevent cervical cancer for women and people with a cervix.
evidence_summary: Cancer Council notes cervical cancer rates have roughly halved since the program began and the renewed program is expected to reduce deaths further, so a strong benefit statement is defensible. The current wording is an unquantified superlative ('most important preventive health check') presented as benefit without limits.
limitations: Benefit stated without noting screening limitations (screening reduces but does not eliminate risk; symptoms still need separate assessment). The recommended wording ties the benefit to its mechanism (preventing cervical cancer) and softens the superlative while keeping the warm, first-person-adjacent voice.
reviewer_notes: Low-urgency softening. AHPRA advertising guidance cautions against unqualified superlatives; framing the benefit around cancer prevention is safer. The article already states elsewhere that symptoms need separate review, which mitigates the limits concern. [Implemented 2026-09-20; applied to site - see corresponding IND entry.]

page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claim_text: Screening is for people without symptoms. If you have symptoms such as bleeding after sex, bleeding between periods, pelvic pain or unusual discharge, you should book a GP review even if you are not due for routine screening.
evidence_summary: Consistent with program guidance that screening is for asymptomatic people and that symptomatic presentations (especially postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding) need separate assessment. This is a key safety message and is correctly stated.
limitations: None; strongly protective wording.

page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claim_text: Long-acting reversible methods such as implants and IUDs are among the most effective because they do not rely on daily remembering.
evidence_summary: LARCs (implant and IUDs) are the most effective reversible methods (>99% effective) precisely because they remove reliance on daily user action ('set and forget'). The article's 'among the most effective because they do not rely on daily remembering' is accurate and, helpfully, avoids quoting bare percentages.
limitations: No 'typical use vs perfect use' distinction is needed here because the claim is qualitative and correctly attributes effectiveness to independence from daily adherence. If a numeric figure is ever added, it must be labelled and given with typical-use context.
reviewer_notes: Good practice - the article states relative effectiveness without unqualified numbers. If future edits add percentages, flag for typical-use qualification.

page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claim_text: Contraception prevents pregnancy, but most methods do not protect against STIs.
evidence_summary: healthdirect states condoms are the only contraceptive method that also helps prevent STIs; all hormonal and intrauterine methods provide no STI protection. 'Most methods do not protect against STIs' is accurate.
limitations: None; important safety message.

page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claim_text: Emergency contraception: Contraception used after unprotected sex or contraceptive failure to reduce pregnancy risk.
evidence_summary: Accurate definition of emergency contraception (oral EC or copper IUD used after unprotected sex or method failure to reduce pregnancy risk). 'Reduce pregnancy risk' correctly avoids implying it is fully effective.
limitations: None; 'reduce' is the correct verb (EC is not 100% effective).

page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claim_text: Can contraception help heavy or painful periods? Some methods can reduce bleeding or pain, but the right choice depends on the cause of symptoms and your medical history.
evidence_summary: Hormonal methods (combined pill, hormonal IUD) can reduce heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhoea for many people. 'Some methods can reduce ... depends on the cause' is accurate and appropriately conditional.
limitations: None; correctly conditional ('can', 'depends on the cause').

page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claim_text: Dr Amanda Henderson is trained in Implanon insertion and removal and Mirena removal.
evidence_summary: This is a claim about the practitioner's own training and scope of practice, not a clinical fact verifiable against external literature. It must be substantiated by internal records (training certificates, CPD/procedural logs). It cannot be verified from public authoritative sources and should not be.
limitations: Not verifiable externally by design. The stated scope is internally consistent with the companion article, which says IUD insertion is referred rather than performed - so no scope overstatement is apparent.
reviewer_notes: AHPRA advertising flag: under the National Law (s.133) and AHPRA advertising guidelines, claims about qualifications, training and services must be accurate, verifiable and not misleading. Confirm Dr Henderson holds current, documented competency in Implanon (Nexplanon) insertion/removal and Mirena removal, and that records are on file. Ensure the site does not imply IUD insertion is offered on-site if it is referral-only (the current wording correctly does not). No legal conclusion drawn.

page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claim_text: Can I use contraception while breastfeeding? Yes, but not every method is suitable at every stage.
evidence_summary: Consistent with medical eligibility guidance: several methods (e.g. progestogen-only pill, implant, IUD, condoms) are suitable during breastfeeding, while combined hormonal methods are generally avoided in the early postpartum period. 'Not every method is suitable at every stage' is accurate and appropriately conditional.
limitations: None; directs the specifics to an individual GP assessment.

page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claim_text: Hormonal IUD: A device placed inside the uterus that releases hormone and can reduce bleeding for many people.
evidence_summary: The hormonal (levonorgestrel) IUD reduces menstrual bleeding for many users and is used to manage heavy menstrual bleeding. 'Can reduce bleeding for many people' is accurate and appropriately hedged.
limitations: None; 'can ... for many people' avoids over-promising a universal effect.

page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claim_text: Copper IUD: A non-hormonal intrauterine device that can also be used for emergency contraception in some circumstances.
evidence_summary: The copper IUD is non-hormonal and can be used as emergency contraception when inserted within the recommended window (about 5 days) after unprotected sex. 'In some circumstances' correctly reflects the timing/eligibility limits.
limitations: None; appropriately qualified.

page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claim_text: Copper IUDs are non-hormonal but can make periods heavier or more painful for some.
evidence_summary: Heavier and/or more painful periods are a recognised side effect of the copper IUD for some users. Accurate and hedged with 'for some'.
limitations: None.

page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claim_text: Will an implant or IUD affect future fertility? Fertility usually returns after removal, although timing can vary.
evidence_summary: Fertility returns rapidly after removal of the implant or IUD, with normal return to baseline fertility; timing of the first ovulation/cycle can vary between individuals. 'Usually returns ... timing can vary' is accurate and appropriately non-absolute.
limitations: None; correctly avoids guaranteeing an outcome or timeframe.

page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claim_text: Is irregular bleeding normal with Implanon? Bleeding changes are common. They may settle, but persistent or troublesome bleeding should be reviewed.
evidence_summary: Unpredictable/irregular bleeding is the most common side effect of the etonogestrel implant and a leading reason for discontinuation; it may improve over time. Accurate, with an appropriate 'should be reviewed' safety net.
limitations: 'Common' is unquantified but epidemiologically accurate for the implant.

page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claim_text: Can a hormonal IUD help heavy periods? For many people it can reduce bleeding, but suitability depends on the cause of bleeding and your medical history.
evidence_summary: The levonorgestrel IUD is an established first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding and reduces bleeding for many users. Wording is accurate and correctly conditions suitability on cause and history.
limitations: None; appropriately hedged.

page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claim_text: Do I still need condoms? Condoms are still important for STI protection ... because implants and IUDs do not protect against STIs.
evidence_summary: Implants and IUDs provide no STI protection; condoms remain necessary for STI risk reduction. Accurate and an important safety message.
limitations: None.

page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claim_text: Dr Amanda Henderson is trained in Implanon insertion and removal and Mirena removal. If you need an IUD insertion she can discuss referral options.
evidence_summary: Practitioner scope-of-practice statement; substantiate against internal training/competency records. Not externally verifiable and should not be. The paired 'IUD insertion ... discuss referral options' correctly signals that IUD insertion is not performed on-site, so scope is not overstated.
limitations: Not externally verifiable by design.
reviewer_notes: AHPRA advertising flag (as WHS-18): ensure the training claim is documented and current, and that the removal-only vs insertion scope for IUDs is not misread by patients. The current referral caveat is good practice. No legal conclusion drawn.

page_title: Sexual Health, Vaginal Symptoms and STI Testing: A GP Visit Should Feel Safe
claim_text: Can I have an STI without symptoms? Yes. Many STIs can be silent, so testing can be useful after new partners or possible exposure.
evidence_summary: healthdirect confirms you can have an STI without noticing symptoms and that testing may be recommended even without symptoms (e.g. after a new partner). Many STIs (notably chlamydia) are frequently asymptomatic. Accurate.
limitations: None; important care-seeking message.

page_title: Sexual Health, Vaginal Symptoms and STI Testing: A GP Visit Should Feel Safe
claim_text: Symptoms may be due to thrush, bacterial vaginosis, STIs, dermatitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, hormonal changes, contraception, menopause or other causes. Guessing can lead to the wrong treatment.
evidence_summary: The listed differential for vaginal symptoms is clinically accurate and the message that self-diagnosis/pharmacy self-treatment can be wrong (especially for recurrent symptoms) is sound and safety-promoting.
limitations: None; the article avoids diagnostic certainty and encourages assessment.

page_title: Sexual Health, Vaginal Symptoms and STI Testing: A GP Visit Should Feel Safe
claim_text: Self-collected swab: A swab taken by the patient after instructions, suitable for some tests. ... Testing may include self-collected swabs, urine tests, blood tests or examination depending on symptoms and risk.
evidence_summary: Self-collected vaginal swabs and first-void urine are validated sample types for certain STI tests (e.g. chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT); the appropriate test depends on symptoms and risk. 'Suitable for some tests' is accurate and does not overstate applicability.
limitations: None; correctly limited with 'for some tests'.

page_title: Sexual Health, Vaginal Symptoms and STI Testing: A GP Visit Should Feel Safe
claim_text: Can recurrent thrush be something else? Yes. Recurrent symptoms may be thrush, bacterial vaginosis, dermatitis, hormonal changes or another condition, so review is worthwhile.
evidence_summary: Recurrent 'thrush' is frequently misdiagnosed and may represent BV, dermatitis, hormonal/atrophic changes or other conditions; review before repeated self-treatment is appropriate advice. Accurate and safety-promoting.
limitations: None.

page_title: Sexual Health, Vaginal Symptoms and STI Testing: A GP Visit Should Feel Safe
claim_text: Avoid using vaginal creams or douches before the appointment if possible because they can affect testing.
evidence_summary: Intravaginal products and douching before sampling can interfere with swab/microscopy results; avoiding them beforehand is standard, sensible preparation advice. Accurate and low-risk.
limitations: None.
